docs.title: SARK V6.5
docs.text:
SARK is a PBX workbench for the popular Asterisk PBX. The current release should be installed onto a host Ubuntu 24.04 server image.

The Documentation in these pages covers how to install the packages which make up SARK.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
V6.5 replaces V6.0 and all previous releases. It can be installed onto X86 or ARM platforms. Only 64-bit architectures are supported. It will happily install on bare-metal or in virtual environments and has additional support for AWS EC2 instances. SARK is developed on Ubuntu and it should ideally be installed onto that distro but you may be able to install it onto other "debian-like" distros (YMMV).

  • It will work with most modern browsers.
  • It will NOT work on any browser that doesn't support jQuery or has it disabled.
  • It will NOT work on any browser that does not support HTML5 or CSS3.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text: V6.5 is designed to run as an appliance and must not be installed onto a multi-purpose system that has other software already installed on it. If you try, you will likely break both the existing systems and SARK. You must begin with an Ubuntu 24.04 minimal install which contains nothing but an SSH server.

docs.title: Installing the package manager
docs.text:
SARK uses the packagecloud repo. Here are the steps you need to prepare to use it.

sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade
curl -s https://packagecloud.io/install/repositories/aelintra/SARK65/script.deb.sh | sudo bash

docs.title: SARK 6.5 Installation
docs.text: The latest SARK 6.5 will auto-install on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (Noble Numbat). It may install on other debian-like releases, but you will need to grab the deb packages from GitHub and install them manually (https://github.com/aelintra/sail65).

docs.title: Installing a Mail Agent
docs.text:
If this is a new install, you should install a mail agent. SARK has on-board support for a lightweight mail agent called ssmtp. If you install it, then SARK will provide a tab in the networking section for you to configure it. Install it now (so that SARK can set the correct permissions) ...:

sudo apt install ssmtp
sudo chmod +x /etc/ssmtp

docs.title: Install MySQL/Mariadb
docs.text:
SARK uses an SQL database to process call statistics. It can be either mysql or mariadb but SARK does not specify which, so you'll need to decide. If in doubt, choose mariadb. Install it now ... 

sudo apt install mariadb-server

OR

sudo apt install mysql-server

N.B. DO NOT run mysql_secure_installation yet!! The SARK install will automatically build the CDR Database for you but it needs access to mysql root without a password. Once the installation is done, you should then run mysql_secure_installation to secure your DB instance (see below).

docs.title: Install iptables
docs.text:
Ubuntu 24.04 favours ufw, SARK uses shorewall with iptables. so... disable ufw and install iptables.

sudo systemctl disable --now ufw
sudo apt update
sudo apt install iptables iptables-persistent

docs.title: Install the SARK packages
docs.text:
sudo apt install sail

The install will take a good few minutes depending upon the speed of the donor box and your internet speed. During the install, you may be asked to enter an admin password for LDAP (make a note of it, you'll need it later if you decide to deploy LDAP as a phone directory). It will also ask about dumpcap but just take the default (No) and let the install run to its conclusion.

docs.title: Reboot
docs.text:
Now reboot your new PBX:

sudo reboot

docs.title: Install Asterisk Extra Sounds Package
docs.text:
SARK requires the Asterisk extra sounds package. If you want UK English, there is a deb on the repo:

sudo apt install ast-en-gb-gpl-gsm-sounds

If you want "Alison" (US American), there is no deb available for this but it's pretty easy to install. At the Linux CLI, do the following:

cd /usr/share/asterisk/sounds
sudo wget http://downloads.asterisk.org/pub/telephony/sounds/asterisk-extra-sounds-en-gsm-current.tar.gz
sudo tar xvfz asterisk-extra-sounds-en-gsm-current.tar.gz
sudo rm asterisk-extra-sounds-en-gsm-current.tar.gz

docs.title: Check and secure your mysql/mariadb database
docs.text:
To check the db is good you can do the following:-

sudo mysql -u root

check the cdr database has been created:- 

show databases;

| Database           |
+--------------------+
| asterisk           |
| information_schema |
| mysql              |
| performance_schema |

+--------------------+
5 rows in set (0.01 sec)

use asterisk
describe cdr;

| Field       | Type         | Null | Key | Default   | Extra             |
+-------------+--------------+------+-----+-----------+-------------------+
| calldate    | datetime     | NO   | MUL | curdate() | DEFAULT_GENERATED |
| clid        | varchar(80)  | NO   |     |           |                   |
| src         | varchar(80)  | NO   |     |           |                   |
| dst         | varchar(80)  | NO   | MUL |           |                   |
| dcontext    | varchar(80)  | NO   |     |           |                   |
| channel     | varchar(80)  | NO   |     |           |                   |
| dstchannel  | varchar(80)  | NO   |     |           |                   |
| lastapp     | varchar(80)  | NO   |     |           |                   |
| lastdata    | varchar(80)  | NO   |     |           |                   |
| duration    | int          | NO   |     | 0         |                   |
| billsec     | int          | NO   |     | 0         |                   |
| disposition | varchar(45)  | NO   |     |           |                   |
| amaflags    | int          | NO   |     | 0         |                   |

15 rows in set (0.00 sec)

If you get the same output as above, you're golden.

Now you can run the secure script for your mysql or maria database

sudo mysql_secure_installation
Follow the script prompts.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
If you were running a previous version of SARK on your browser then you will need to clear your browser cache or open an incognito/private window before proceeding. If you don't, you'll get odd-looking output as the cached jQuery code fights with the new V6.5 output.

Your SARK app will be at https://your.server.ip.address

Default login credentials will be...

  • UID: admin
  • PWD: sarkadmin

The SARK browser application will force you to change your password on first login. This will change BOTH the browser AND linux root passwords.

docs.title: LDAP
docs.text: If you wish to use SARK's LDAP support to provide directory lookups to your phones, proceed as follows:

docs.title: Check the LDAP Base Name (Base DN)
docs.text:
You can check by running slapcat as follows:

sudo slapcat

dn: dc=nodomain
objectClass: top
objectClass: dcObject
objectClass: organization
o: nodomain
dc: nodomain

The base name appears in the first line of output. In the above example, it is "dc=nodomain". We've used "nodomain" as an example because you'll likely see it a lot, particularly when you are spinning up LXC instances and the like. It just means that LDAP couldn't find the FQDN, probably because it wasn't set. It's no big deal, you can just go ahead and use dc=nodomain if you like. In any event, you should enter whatever YOUR base name is into the Globals=>LDAP panel along with the LDAP password you chose during the install. If "dc=nodomain" bothers you, then you'll need to enter a domain name in SARK, issue a commit and then do a reconfigure for slapd (the LDAP daemon):

sudo dpkg-reconfigure slapd

This will allow it to have another look.

docs.title: Adding the Contacts OU
docs.text:
Now we need to add an organizationalUnit (ou) for the address book. If you are already a whiz with LDAP, then just go ahead and do it, using the base name. If you don't know LDAP, then proceed as follows:

You will find a file on your SARK box at /opt/sark/cache/ldapcontactou.ldif:

dn: ou=contacts,dc=sark,dc=aelintra,dc=com
objectClass: organizationalUnit
objectClass: top
ou: contacts

Without getting into the details (you can read about LDAP elsewhere); in the first line of the file is the name of the organizationalUnit we want to create. In our example, it is "contacts". The remainder of the line (dc=sark,dc=aelintra,dc=com) is the base name we discussed earlier. You must edit the file to make the file match your base name from the slapcat you did a couple of steps back. If, for example, you have a base name of dc=splodge,dc=soap,dc=com then you should make your file look like this:

dn: ou=contacts,dc=splodge,dc=soap,dc=com
objectClass: organizationalUnit
objectClass: top
ou: contacts

Ok, let's add it. We are going to use the LDAP slapadd utility, which is old-fashioned nowadays, but easy to use:

sudo service slapd stop
sudo slapadd -l /opt/sark/cache/ldapcontactou.ldif
sudo service slapd start

Refresh your browser and navigate to SARK. You should see a "Directory" option when you click on the "Settings" drop-down. In this page, you can add and modify your telephone book entries or upload a vCard file you have exported from Google contacts or whatever. You can also have your phones browse your contacts if you have SIP phones which are LDAP aware (many are). You'll need to add a couple of entries to your SARK firewall for TCP ports 389 and 686 (restrict them to net:$LAN) to allow the phones to query the database - don't forget to restart the firewall.

docs.title: Set Up Your Phones to Use LDAP
docs.text: Most major SIP Phone types can use LDAP; however, the implementation varies from type to type. Snom, Panasonic (KX-HDV), Yealink, and Fanvil all support LDAP and have on-board provisioning already set up for openLDAP on SARK. Cisco small business phones (SPA) support LDAP and Provu have a section on their website showing how to set them up here. Polycom phone set-up is more complex (isn't it always?), however, there is good documentation provided by Polycom so you should be able to get it running with a little work although we don't show it here. Gigaset professional (N series) phones support LDAP and there is documentation on their website.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
The SARKV65 firewall uses the Shorewall firewall.

Below is a screenshot of the firewall from a newly installed system.

N.B. ports 80, 443 and 22 are initially set open to anywhere. This is so you don't accidentally lock yourself out before you begin. You MUST restrict these to a sensible set of values before you go live with the system. Usually, as a first step, net:$LAN (see below) might be sufficient. Obviously, if you are accessing the system from outside the LAN then you'll need to handle that too.

Any cell rendered in blue can be inline edited by clicking on it and modifying the contents. Once done, click away (i.e. outside the edit box.)

Create a new rule by clicking the +Add button at the top of the screen.

docs.title: Source
docs.text:
Source will always begin net. If you type nothing else than the rule will be worldwide accessible (so be careful with it). To narrow the permission, follow net with a colon (net:) and then a source. The source can be specified in CIDR format or as an absolute IP address.

So, if you wanted to restrict access to a rule from IP address 5.5.5.5 (and ONLY 5.5.5.5), then you could code

net:5.5.5.5

or

net:5.5.5.5/32, which is the same thing.

There is a special value, $LAN, which allows access from your local subnet (e.g. 192.168.0.0/16, 172.16.0.0/12, 10.0.0.0/8 etc.). The actual subnet is harvested by SARK when it initializes.

net:$LAN

docs.title: Protocol
docs.text: This is a dropdown which can either udp or tcp

docs.title: Ports
docs.text:
This can be a single port, mutiple ports (separated by commas) and/or a port range (separated by a colon). So, for example to handle SIP/RTP UDP you might code

5060,10000:20000

This would handle both SIP (5060) and RTP range (10000:20000)

docs.title: Rate
docs.text: This controls the connection rate of an endpoint. It is specified as the maximum number of allowed connections per time unit. So, the rule 4/min:5, in the default SIP (5060) rule, allows a burst of 5 connections per source IP and 4 connections per minute. You can find full details of this in the Shorewall docs.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: This is a freeform description strin which yu can include next to the rule. Use plain language without special characters, e.g. SIP from the London Office

docs.title: Apply your changes
docs.text: Hit the Restart Firewall button at the top of the page. This will give you a report on how well your changes went. Any errors will be flagged and the firewall will not be restarted. Go back to the firewall page and correct any errors.

docs.title: Upgrade from an earlier version
docs.text: SARK upgrades are handled via migration. In other words, you create a new bare server install of SARK V6.5 and then load a backup from a previous version. This will usually work without issue for all V6.x releases. It may work for prevous V5.x releases but YMMV. It's important to note that V6.5 uses the PJSIP module in Asterisk and this may have implications if you have any custom apps (or your own custom code) which, for example, dial SIP/. You should examine your custom apps to ensure that any such occurrences are updated to dial PJSIP/ instead.

docs.title: Step 1
docs.text:
Create a new instance according to the Installation section. Once you have your new instance and can login to it you are ready to migrate the old system forward.

Top Tip - Assuming you are working with a VM instance (and you should be for testing), take a snapshot of your clean-install system before proceeding. This will allow you to quickly recover in case of accidents later in the process.

docs.title: Step 2
docs.text: Download a recent backup from your old system to your workstation. You will use this to create the new system

docs.title: Step 3
docs.text:
Login to the new system and navigate to Settings->Backup/Restore. Click the Upload button at the top right of the panel to load your backup to the new system. The backup will appear in the Saved Backups list. Click the restore icon for that backup set. Restore the following sections

  • Sark database
  • Voicemail
  • usergreetings
  • LDAP (if required)

Do NOT restore the Asterisk folder

docs.title: Step 4
docs.text:
Issue a Commit

N.B. Backups do not contain firewall rules so you will need to recreate them on the new instance.

Once you have set the firewall to your taste, reboot the instance,

You now should have your new 6.5 system ready to test.
